title: Psalm 14 - The Foolish Heart
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This lesson examines Psalm 14's description of the fool who denies God's existence and the universal human condition of depravity apart from Christ. The speaker contrasts the fool with the wise, explains that no one naturally seeks God, and concludes with the encouraging truth that salvation comes entirely from God's grace through Christ.

outline.title: The Nature of the Fool
subpoints: The fool is contrasted with the wise and the simple in Scripture
The fool has been instructed in God's Word but refuses to live according to it
The fool's sin against knowledge is more heinous than the sin of the ignorant
The practical atheist is the only atheist that exists; all people know God exists but choose to deny it

outline.title: The Depravity of Humanity
subpoints: God looks down and finds no one who understands or seeks Him
All humanity apart from Christ has turned aside and become corrupt
No one naturally seeks the true God
There is no innate goodness in humanity; all are incapable of moral good apart from God

outline.title: The Corruption of the Fool
subpoints: The fool is disfigured from God's design, not functioning as created
The fool commits vile deeds contrary to God's law
Even the best acts of unbelievers are like dirty rags before God
This is the doctrine of total depravity—man is corrupt in every aspect of his being

outline.title: The Problem with Seeker-Friendly Ministry
subpoints: No one seeks the true God by nature
Making churches seeker-friendly makes them worldly without attracting the world effectively
Whatever attracts people to church is what they come seeking, not Christ

outline.title: Salvation Comes from God Alone
subpoints: Children of man cannot turn to God on their own; salvation must come from outside
Salvation comes from Zion—from God who dwells in His holy hill
God's righteousness is revealed through faith in Jesus Christ
God justifies freely by His grace through Christ's redemption

outline.title: Three Encouragements from Total Depravity
subpoints: We are powerless to save ourselves but also powerless to unsave ourselves; God keeps us in His hands
Salvation is entirely God's work; He calls us to Himself by His Spirit
Since all salvation is God's work and God is all-powerful, we are in the best situation possible

transcript:
## Reading Scripture

> "To the chief musician, a Psalm of David, the fool has said in his heart, there is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none who does good. The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek God, they have all turned aside, they have together become corrupt, there's none who does good, no not one. Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge who eat up the people as they eat bread and do not call on the Lord? There they are in great fear for God is with the generation of the righteous. You shame the counsel of the poor but the Lord is his refuge. Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion when the Lord brings back the captivity of his people that Jacob rejoiced and Israel be glad." (Psalm 14)

Except with minor differences, Psalm 14 is the same as Psalm 53. It is a Psalm of David, but verse 7, if you notice, is something that was added later on by the inspiration of the Spirit, either during or after the Babylonian captivity. As with so many of David's psalms, we can't really tell when and why it was written or trace it to an event of David's life. Perhaps this is just David's musings as he's thought about what it means to be a fool and to not follow the Lord.

## The Description of the Fool

What you see here is a description of the fool. In verse 1, David says, "The fool says in his heart there is no God." The scriptural fool is always cast in contrast with the wise. The fool is the wicked sinner while the wise is the redeemed righteous.

### The Difference Between the Fool and the Simple

There's also a great difference between the fool and the simple in the Bible. The simple is the ignorant, the one who needs to be instructed in the Word of God. Remember what Psalm 19 says in verse 7: "The law of the Lord is perfect converting the soul, the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple." So the simple is the uninstructed, is the ignorant, the one that doesn't know.

The fool is the one who has been instructed in the Word of God and does not live according to it. An example of that in the book of Proverbs is Proverbs 15:5 where it says, "A fool despises his father's instruction."

### The Sin of the Fool Versus the Sin of the Simple

When the simple and the fool transgress or don't conform to the law of God, they both sin. However, the sin of the fool is much more heinous, much worse than the sin of the simple because it is sin against knowledge.

The fool lives as if there is no God according to David. He or she continually says in his or her heart that there is no God, and he does that in order to convince himself that there isn't a God so that his conscience won't bother him. He does that at the heart level because the heart controls everything in life.

As Proverbs says, "Keep your heart with all diligence because out of it flow all the issues of life." The fool teaches us the importance of guarding our hearts by being very careful about how we think and what we think. Proverbs 23 says, "For as he thinks in his heart so is he."

### The Practical Atheist

It is important for us to notice that David describes the atheistic fool in terms of what he does. Do you notice that? The fool does this and this, not in terms of who he is, and there's a reason for that. David does that because the practical atheist is the only atheist that exists. There's no such thing as one who in his heart or her heart is an atheist.

The Bible tells us that according to the scriptures, everyone knows that there is a God, but some choose to live as if that God didn't exist. In Romans 1 verses 20 to 23, the apostle Paul says:

> "For since the creation of the world his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse. Because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God nor were thankful but became futile in their thoughts and their foolish hearts were darkened." (Romans 1:20-23)

Why is everyone without excuse? Because although they knew God, everyone who sees creation, everyone who experiences creation, they see God. There's no such thing as a naturally atheistic person by nature. Their heart was darkened because they were fools in denying that there is a God.

## The Practice of the Fool

Now notice in verse one, he says, "The fool has said in his heart," (singular) but then he continues and goes on to plural verbs: "there is no God, they are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none who does good."

David goes from a singular noun and verb in the first line of verse one to plural nouns and verbs in the rest of the verse because the word "fool" in verse one is a collective word. It includes all the fools. He's not just thinking of that one guy. He's talking about the entirety of humanity apart from Christ that denies the existence of God.

He says the fool is corrupt, and the idea here is that the fool is depraved or disfigured. Just to use an illustration: have you ever been to those halls of mirrors where you walk in and you are too short, too skinny, too fat, too wide, too crooked? That's the fool—a disfigurement of the design of God. It's one who is not functioning as God created him to function. All of us were created to know God and to glorify him and to enjoy him in that process. Yet the fool who says there is no God has been disfigured, corrupted, twisted. This shows that the state of foolishness is not what God designed for us. It is a corruption of what God intended.

### The Fool's Deeds

David says that the fool had committed vile deeds, deeds that are contrary to the law of God. If you go and look at the book of Proverbs and search for the word "fool," you're going to find verse after verse that talks about the fool, and you can very truthfully replace the word "fool" with the word "sinner" and the meaning of the passages won't change.

David tells us that the fool is incapable of doing good, any moral good. Anyone who lives as if there is no God is incapable of doing moral good. You might protest: "That's not true. I know unbelievers who do good; they feed the poor and so on." Yet Isaiah tells us that the best of our acts, the best of our righteousness, is nothing more than dirty rags before the eyes of God because it's tainted by sin.

Brothers and sisters, the supreme good is trusting God. And if you don't have that, then everything that comes from you is not morally good.

## The Universal Verdict of Depravity

In verses two and three, the Lord declares that every child of man is a fool by nature. Look at verse two: "The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek God, they have all turned aside, they have together become corrupt, there's none who does good, no, not one."

Here God changes the perspective from the particular (the fool) to the universal (the fools, or the children of man), because He says both are the same. Anyone apart from Christ is the fool of Psalm 14 because any belief that is not a belief in the God of the Bible is an atheistic belief. There's no other God. And if you're not trusting in that God, the God of the Bible, you're not trusting in any God at all. And therefore you are an atheist who says in his heart, "There is no God," which the Bible calls the fool.

### God's Perpetual Looking

The translation does a good job when it renders the first Hebrew verb in verse two with the present tense English verb "looks." The Lord looks down from heaven. This is technically a past tense, but in context it works as a present tense. The looking on God's part is not something He did once and that was it. But God is perennially always looking down to see if there's any who do good. It's a constant quest of God to find that one person who is seeking Him, who is seeking to do what is good.

Every time that God looks down from heaven, it's not because He is seeing something good going on. There are only three other times in the Bible where this expression is used, and that's not because God's seeing some good stuff. The first is in Genesis 6, the flood, and what does He see when He looked down from heaven? That the intents of man's heart were continually evil.

The second time is the Tower of Babel. And remember He says He looked down. Man says, "Oh, we're going to build a building that's going to go all the way up to heaven. Oh, we're so good. Our ingenuity is great. We're going to build this tower on our own. We're going to reach heaven. We're going to go to God independently of God." And God says, "Oh, let me just look down. Look down there. That tiny little tower down there. They were supposed to reach up to the heavens."

And the third time that God came and looked down was in Sodom and Gomorrah, where God looks down and sees what He sees there. This indicates here that God is going to judge the fool. When He looks down at man, He is looking down in judgment.

This anthropomorphic representation of God with the human characteristics of looking down teaches us two things that God is looking for in the children of man. Look at verse two again: "The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek God."

He's looking for any who understand. That's the first thing. What is the object of understanding? What is it that God is trying to find somebody understanding? I think the answer is the law of God. The man who understands is the wise man because he lives according to his knowledge. God wants us, the children of man, to be wise people.

And the second thing is looking to see if there's any who seeks after Him. To seek God is to pursue Him, to know Him, to rely on Him like the Psalmist in Psalm 63 where he says, "Oh God, you are my God. Early I will seek you, my soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you in a dry and thirsty land where there is no water." God is looking down and seeking for people who are doing that kind of seeking after Him. God wants us, children of man, to seek after Him.

### The Absence of Seekers

And yet the Psalmist says that he did not find any of that. In verse three: "They all have turned aside, they have together become corrupt. There is none who does good. No, not one."

As God looks down at the children of man, He does not find any who understand or seek Him. Notice now the scope is expanded. It is not only the fool that lives as if there is no God, it is also all apart from the grace of God who live as if there is no God. If a person lives not according to God's Word, they are living as if there is no God. If you live apart from obedience to God, you are living—no matter what you claim—you're living as if there is no God.

And notice also that God does not find anyone who is seeking Him. That's the sad conclusion of this verse. They find none. This statement has tremendous implications for how we deal with unbelievers. We cannot make our goal to make everything in church seeker-friendly because no one seeks the true God.

### The Problem with Seeker-Friendly Churches

What ends up happening when this is our attempt is that we end up making the church just like the world so that the world can feel comfortable in it. The problem is that the church stinks being like the world. We do a very poor job of being the world, so we're never going to attract the world with the world. On top of that, whatever we attract people with, that's what we attract them to. And if we want to give them what they're seeking, that is not going to be Jesus Christ, the Savior, the Forgiver of their sins.

### Universal Depravity

All the children of man have turned aside, David says in verse three, or have literally departed. This happened at the Fall, and this is true of everyone of us since then. There isn't one soul in this world who is seeking God. We know that God made us with a God-shaped hole in our hearts that needs to be filled, and there's truth in that. But we're not seeking to fill that hole with God. We're not seeking naturally to be finding rest in God. We already know that He exists and we've rejected Him in our existence.

David says that all the children of man have become morally corrupt. There isn't any innate goodness in humanity. There's no spark of the divinity in any of us. We are not good. There isn't one person on the face of the earth who does good, apart from the Lord Jesus Christ.

As an example of that in Proverbs 21:4, the Holy Spirit says: "A haughty look, a proud heart, and even the plowing, which is a good thing, right? The plowing of the land—even the plowing of the wicked is sin."

This is a doctrine commonly called the total depravity or the total inability of man. Man is corrupt in every aspect of his being and incapable of doing what is morally good in the sight of God. Paul quoted verses one through three in Romans 3 to prove that all of humanity lies under sin and is therefore subject to the punishment due to it. That's where you are apart from Christ. That's where all of humanity is apart from Christ.

## Salvation from Zion

But verse seven brings a different message. In verse seven, the Holy Spirit says: "Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion when the Lord brings back the captivity of his people. Let Jacob rejoice and Israel be glad."

The children of man, namely us, cannot turn to God on our own. So salvation must come from Zion, that is, from outside of us. Who lives in Zion? Jesus. God is in Zion. Zion is His holy hill. And what David is saying is that salvation must come from outside of us. Salvation must come from God.

This is what Paul argues in Romans 3, where in verses 21 through 25 he says:

> "Now the righteousness of God, apart from the law, is revealed, being witnessed by the law and the prophets, even the righteousness of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, to all and on all who believe. For there's no difference. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation by his blood through faith, to demonstrate his righteousness, because in his forbearance God had passed over the sins that were previously committed." (Romans 3:21-25)

God saves. Do you get that? God saves. Do you know what the name is in the Bible? Jesus—Yahweh saves. God saves.

The doctrine of the total depravity of man is a biblical one, taken out of Psalm 14. And it may seem discouraging. You might say, "I stayed for a warm Sunday afternoon just for him to tell me that I'm bad and not in a good way, right? Because it can be bad in a good way, but this is bad in a bad way."

## Three Encouragements from Total Depravity

But if you stop and think, this is an encouraging doctrine when you give it a little thought. Let me give you three encouragements from this doctrine.

### First Encouragement: We Cannot Unsave Ourselves

The first one is this: We are powerless to save ourselves. I said, wait a minute, I thought you're still going to encourage us. We are powerless to save ourselves, but we also are powerless to unsave ourselves. The God who saves also causes you to persevere, because there's nothing, absolutely nothing that can separate you from the love of God in Jesus Christ. Do you get that, brother and sister? The same God that turned your heart to Him is the God who keeps that heart in His hands.

### Second Encouragement: Salvation is Entirely God's Work

Secondly, since we are completely unable to save ourselves, salvation must entirely be the work of God. He must call us to Himself by His Spirit. And brothers and sisters, He does just that. Do you need evidence of that? You're here. You're a believer in Jesus Christ. He called you to Him. And if, especially if you are saved from outside of the church, you know that it took God to save you. It wasn't because you're such a great person or whatever. More than likely you're running in the opposite direction and God caused you to come to Him.

### Third Encouragement: God is All-Powerful and Faithful

And thirdly, since it is all the work of God, and God is all powerful and does what He wants, and He never changes, and He has promised to save His people, we are in the best situation we could be in. We can't do anything to save ourselves, but God can and He will. He said that all that the Father has given to the Son will come to the Son. And the Son will in no way cast them out.

So praise the Lord for His grace that saves people like us. And with Paul, all of us can say that we're the chief of sinners. And yet God saves even the chiefest of sinners.
